Chapter 6 Thermal Conductance Measurements

In this appendix, we will discuss the principles of how we can measure thermal conductances with TESs and measure the conductances for various systems.

Appendix 6.A Thermal Conductance Measurement Principles with TESs

The general setup for an arbitrary TES in a dilution refrigerator is pictured in Fig. F.1. There is a TES on an absorber, which itself is connected to the thermal bath (e.g. through detector holders or through a thermalizing Au wire bond). There is also some type of heater that can change the temperature of the thermal bath. Since the TES is in thermal contact with an absorber, which is in thermal contact with the bath, we must measure two thermal conductances, GT​AG_{TA} and GA​BG_{AB}, to understand the thermal properties of our system. In the following sections, we explain the principles behind the measurements of these two values.

1 Measuring Thermal Conductance between Absorber and Bath

We begin with measuring GA​BG_{AB}, which requires two TESs on the same absorber, one which acts as an absorber thermometer and the other as an absorber heater. The underlying equation that we want to fit is

PA​B=KA​B​(Tan−Tbn),P_{AB}=K_{AB}(T_{a}^{n}-T_{b}^{n}), (1)

where PA​BP_{AB} is the power flowing from absorber to bath, TaT_{a} is the temperature of the absorber, TbT_{b} is the temperature of the bath, nn is a power-law exponent, and KA​BK_{AB} is related to GA​BG_{AB} via

GA​B=d​PA​Bd​Ta=n​KA​B​Tan−1.G_{AB}=\frac{dP_{AB}}{dT_{a}}=nK_{AB}T_{a}^{n-1}. (2)

To extract GA​BG_{AB}, we must fit Eq. (1), which requires measuring PA​BP_{AB} as a function of TbT_{b}, while keeping TaT_{a} constant. Because these measurements will be made when the system is in thermal equilibrium, the power flowing from the TESs to the absorber will be equal to the power flowing from the absorber to the bath. Thus, we can bias a TES in the normal regime with a Joule heating of

PT​E​S=IT​E​S2​RN,P_{TES}=I_{TES}^{2}R_{N}, (3)

where IT​E​SI_{TES} is the current flowing through the TES and RNR_{N} is the TES normal resistance, both of which can be known through the characterization steps outlined in Chapter 1. The TES current can be related back to the bias current Ib​i​a​sI_{bias} and various resistances of the system via

IT​E​S=Ib​i​a​s​Rs​hRℓ+RN,I_{TES}=I_{bias}\frac{R_{sh}}{R_{\ell}+R_{N}}, (4)

where Rs​hR_{sh} is the shunt resistance, RℓR_{\ell} is the load resistance, and RNR_{N} is the normal resistance.

To measure PA​BP_{AB} as a function of TbT_{b}, we can use a heater placed in the bath (usually the mixing chamber in a dilution refrigerator) and measure the change in power as we change the heat load on the bath. To keep TaT_{a} constant, we use our two TESs that have been fabricated on the same absorber. The thermometer TES is biased at some point in its superconducting transition, such that any change in temperature in the absorber will change the TES bias point. The heater TES is biased such that it is normal, and its Joule heating will heat up the absorber. This setup is diagrammatically shown in Fig. F.2.

The measurement carries out as follows: we bias TES1 low in transition and heat the bath up to a few mK below the TcT_{c} of TES1 (e.g. start at 42​mK42\,\mathrm{mK} if Tc=45​mKT_{c}=45\,\mathrm{mK}), such that biasing TES2 normal will keep TES1 in transition. TES2 is then biased normal with a power that should be much greater than the bias power of TES1, such that the latter can be neglected (this should be simple if TES1 is the more sensitive device). This first point gives PA​BP_{AB} at the starting TbT_{b}, as well as our starting bias point for TES1. We then decrease the heat load on the bath, which decreases TaT_{a} and equivalently changes the bias point of TES1, as the power flowing in equilibrium has not yet changed (it is still equal to the Joule heating of TES2). To remedy this, we increase the bias current on TES2 until TES1 has returned to its initial bias point and thus so has TaT_{a}. This gives us our second data point for PA​BP_{AB} at a new TbT_{b}. This procedure is then continued until either TES2 can no longer heat the absorber up to the same TaT_{a} (due to some limitation with the amount of bias current that can be supplied) or we have reached the base temperature of the dilution refrigerator.

In Fig. F.2, the bias point of TES1 is represented by its response to a square wave. In this case, we would know that, when changing the Joule heating of TES2, TES1 has returned to its initial bias point when zero frequency change of its response (i.e. ∂I/∂V⁡(0)\partial I/\partial V(0)) is the same. Alternatively, an equivalent method is to not send a square wave jitter down the bias line, but instead follow the DC value of the TES current. After the DC value changes as the bath is heated, then TES1 will have returned to its initial point by changing the Joule heating of TES2 until TES1 has the same TES current. It is up to the person doing the measurement which they prefer, the former gives more TES information, while the latter may be faster in terms of data taking time (no need to fit the TES response, but simply track the DC value of the current).

At the conclusion of the measurement, we will have PA​BP_{AB} as function of TbT_{b} at hopefully many bias points, and we can simply fit Eq. (1) via a least squares routine to extract GA​BG_{AB}, TaT_{a}, and nn. It may also be useful to calculate the natural time constant τ=C/GA​B\tau=C/G_{AB} where CC is the heat capacity of the absorber, which is the characteristic time for the absorber to cool back down to base temperature after being warmed up to about TcT_{c} (e.g. a muon hits the detector and pushes the TESs normal). If the absorber is a semiconductor or insulator (usually the case), then we can estimate its heat capacity in the low-temperature Debye limit

Ct​h=12​π4​kb5​A​ρ​V​NA​(TaΘD)3,C^{th}=\frac{12\pi^{4}k_{b}}{5A}\rho VN_{A}\left(\frac{T_{a}}{\Theta_{D}}\right)^{3}, (5)

where kb=1.38×10−23​J/Kk_{b}=1.38\times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{K} is the Boltzmann constant, ρ\rho is the density of the absorber, VV is the volume of the absorber, AA is the atomic mass of the absorber, NA=6.022×1023​mol−1N_{A}=6.022\times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1} is the Avogadro constant, and ΘD\Theta_{D} is the Debye temperature of for the absorber.

2 Measuring Thermal Conductance between TES and Absorber

To measure GT​AG_{TA}, we only need a single TES, but it is dependent on already having done the GA​BG_{AB}. The underlying equation that we want to fit is

PT​A=KT​A​(Tcn−Tan),P_{TA}=K_{TA}(T_{c}^{n}-T_{a}^{n}), (6)

where TcT_{c} is the superconducting critical temperature of the TES, nn is the power law exponent, and KT​AK_{TA} is related to GT​AG_{TA} via

GT​A=d​PT​Ad​Tc=n​KT​A​Tcn−1.G_{TA}=\frac{dP_{TA}}{dT_{c}}=nK_{TA}T_{c}^{n-1}. (7)

As discussed in Section 3.5 of Irwin and Hilton [97], the thermal impedance between the electrons and phonons in a metal with small volume and high power density (e.g. a W TES) dominates. In this case, the power flow is from the electrons to the phonons via P=Σe​p​VT​E​S​(Te​l5−Tp​h5)P=\Sigma_{ep}V_{TES}\left(T_{el}^{5}-T_{ph}^{5}\right), where VT​E​SV_{TES} is the TES volume and Σe​p\Sigma_{ep} is a material-dependent electron-phonon coupling constant (usually on the order of 109​W​m−3​K−510^{9}\,\mathrm{W}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{K}^{-5}). Thus, it is expected that n=5n=5, KT​A=Σe​p​VT​E​SK_{TA}=\Sigma_{ep}V_{TES}, and GT​A=5​Σe​p​VT​E​S​Tc4G_{TA}=5\Sigma_{ep}V_{TES}T_{c}^{4} for a W TES.

Note that Eq. (6) is dependent on TaT_{a}, but the experimental setup generally only has the ability to measure TbT_{b}, showing why it is important to measure GA​BG_{AB} first in order to accurately calculate TaT_{a}. Although, in practice, a good thermal connection between absorber to bath will mean that GA​B≫GT​AG_{AB}\gg G_{TA} and Ta≈TbT_{a}\approx T_{b}. Thus, in single-channel devices (i.e. only one TES channel on an absorber), it is common to make the assumption that Ta≈TbT_{a}\approx T_{b} if the thermalization scheme is known to have a large GA​BG_{AB} from historical measurements and continue to do a GT​AG_{TA} measurement.

For the GT​AG_{TA} measurement, the setup is simple: we have a single TES on a substrate, which is thermally connected to the absorber, and the absorber is thermally connected to the bath. For this measurement, we keep the TES at the same transition point while changing the bath temperature via the heater, and we calculate the TES bias power as a function of bath temperature. Since we wait for the system to reach equilibrium, the bias power of the TES P0P_{0} will be equal to the power from the TES to the absorber PT​AP_{TA}, which in turn is equal to the power from the absorber to the bath PA​BP_{AB}. P0P_{0} is easily defined via

P0=I02​R0,P_{0}=I_{0}^{2}R_{0}, (8)

where I0I_{0} is the current through the TES, and R0R_{0} is TES resistance. There are two common ways to calculate P0P_{0} as a function of TbT_{b} for the GT​AG_{TA} measurement: the “quick” way and the “clean” way.

The Quick GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

The quick measurement is to bias the TES in transition and measure the TES response. If the TES is low enough in transition, then we can use that, in the limit of large loop gain ℒ\mathcal{L}, the TES complex impedance (Eq. (32)) becomes

limℒ→∞Zcirc​(ω)=Rℓ+i​ω​L−R0,\lim_{\mathcal{L}\to\infty}Z_{\mathrm{circ}}(\omega)=R_{\ell}+i\omega L-R_{0}, (9)

and the zero-frequency value is Zcirc​(0)=Rℓ−R0Z_{\mathrm{circ}}(0)=R_{\ell}-R_{0}. Thus, we can solve for R0=|Zcirc​(0)|+RℓR_{0}=\left|Z_{\mathrm{circ}}(0)\right|+R_{\ell} and I0=Ib​i​a​s​Rs​h/(R0+Rℓ)I_{0}=I_{bias}R_{sh}/(R_{0}+R_{\ell}), and we have an estimate of P0P_{0}.

The quick GT​AG_{TA} measurement procedure is then as follows (and pictured in Fig. F.3): we bias the TES low in transition and heat the bath up to a few mK below the TcT_{c} of TES (e.g. start at 42​mK42\,\mathrm{mK} if Tc=45​mKT_{c}=45\,\mathrm{mK}). We measure the zero-frequency value of the circuit complex impedance, and we immediately have an estimate of P0P_{0} and, equivalently, PT​AP_{TA} for at this TbT_{b}. In order to convert this TbT_{b} to TaT_{a} (if we have a GA​BG_{AB} measurement), we use Eq. (2), giving the first data point for PT​AP_{TA} as a function of TaT_{a}. We then, as we did with GA​BG_{AB}, decrease the heat load on the bath, which decreases TaT_{a} and equivalently changes the bias point of the TES, as the power flowing in equilibrium has not yet changed (it is equal to the Joule heating of the TES). Note that the TES in transition is also supplying the Joule heating, in contrast to the GA​BG_{AB} measurement system (in which the in-transition TES bias power was negligible). When we increase the bias current to the TES so that it returns to the same bias point (i.e. the same R0R_{0}) the bias power will increase, and TaT_{a} will decrease. Doing this, we have a second data point for the bias power of the TES as a function of TaT_{a}. This procedure continues until we have reached the base temperature of the dilution refrigerator (that is, the heater on the mixing chamber has zero heat load).

This measurement can go quickly, but the approximation of ℒ→∞\mathcal{L}\to\infty may introduce a systematic on R0R_{0}, and we may actually have a different true bias power. To avoid this possible systematic, the GT​AG_{TA} measurement can be done using clean way, at the expense of longer data taking.

The Clean GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

In essence, the clean GT​AG_{TA} measurement is done by taking I​VIV sweeps at many different bath temperatures. These I​VIV sweeps can then be interpolated such that we can choose the same TES resistance for each bath temperature from the sweep, immediately extracting the measured I0I_{0} and R0R_{0} and avoiding possible systematic error. The drawback is that these I​VIV sweeps take a fair amount of time (perhaps an hour per sweep), depending on how many points are desired. When doing these for many bath temperatures, the data taking time can quickly become nearly the entire day. Because of this, usually the quick way to do the measurement is done first, with the clean way done in the case of analysis for publication. We show an example of the clean way in Section 4.

With our methods of measuring GA​BG_{AB} and GT​AG_{TA} explained, we will next show a few example measurements, where all nonlinear least squares fits are done using optimize.curve_fit in SciPy [224].

Appendix 6.B Thermal Conductance Measurements with G115

Developed by Matt Pyle and Suhas Ganjam, G115 is a prototype detector, consisting of a 3​inch3\,\mathrm{inch} diameter and 1​mm1\,\mathrm{mm} thick Ge wafer, with a four-channel QET mask deposited on one side (mask design shown in Fig. F.4). This detector was made to study QET performance, as well as for understanding the effect high energy events (muons and photons) on high voltage noise, as discussed in detail in Noah Kurinsky’s thesis [114]. In this section, we will bypass that discussion and instead summarize the thermal conductance measurements made on this device in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator as SLAC, in which the detector was thermally connected to bath via cirlex clamps.

For these measurements, we will use two of the inner channels of G115, henceforth known as channels A and B in this section. The measured normal resistances of the channels A and B are 200​m​Ω200\,\mathrm{m}\Omega and 182​m​Ω182\,\mathrm{m}\Omega, respectively. For each channel, the parasitic resistance is Rp=12​m​ΩR_{p}=12\,\mathrm{m}\Omega.

1 Cirlex Clamps

The cirlex clamps holding scheme will have a interfacial thermal resistance due to the elastic constant mismatch between the dissimilar semiconducting substrate and the clamps themselves [95], and the thermal conductance is expected to go as G∝T3G\propto T^{3}.

GA​BG_{AB} Measurement

To measure GA​BG_{AB}, we follow the method as outlined in Section 1, where channel A acted as a thermometer, and channel B acted as a heater. The data from this measurement are reported in Table 1, wherehe error in PA​BP_{AB} is set to be 10% of the measured power, based on an estimated 10% uncertainty in Rs​hR_{sh}. The dominant systematic when taking these measurements was that the fridge had a stabilization time of 𝒪⁡(20​min)\mathcal{O}(20\,\mathrm{min}), meaning that it was difficult to tell if we had fully stabilized at each point. Furthermore, the size of the detector meant that it had a substantial rate of high energy events (muons and gammas) at the surface, which would heat the substrate. Thus, there may be some bias in the measurements, which is difficult to quantify.

We next fit Eq. (2) with nn allowed to be any value, and n=4n=4 fixed as expected from the phonon mismatch between the absorber and the clamps. In Fig. F.5, we show the results of these two fits and compare to the measured data, with the various fit parameters reported in Table 2. It is clear from the fits that we did not take enough data (i.e. go to a low enough bath temperature) to be able to describe the power law behavior with any confidence. However, the thermal conductance itself is not very sensitive to the power law exponent, nor is the absorber temperature, so we were still able to estimate the absorber heat capacity and the thermal time constant to a reasonable degree.

GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

To measure GT​AG_{TA}, we used channel A and the quick GT​AG_{TA} measurement method (i.e. estimating the TES resistance from the zero-frequency value of the circuit impedance). The data from this measurement are reported in Table 3, and the error in PT​AP_{TA} is estimated to be 10% of the measured power. The sources of systematic error are the same as the discussion for the GA​BG_{AB} measurement, such that there may be a bias in these measurements due to the long thermalization times of the fridge and the high rate of high-energy events.

Using Eq. (7), we fit the power law with nn varying and n=5n=5 fixed, the latter as expected for a W TES. In Fig. F.6, we show the results of the two fits as compared to the measured data, and report the various fit parameters in Table 4. With this data, we took enough data points, but we instead have an anomalous power exponent of n=3.1±0.5n=3.1\pm 0.5 when letting nn vary. As this is far from expectation, and we know that we were having trouble with the long fridge thermalization times, we can explain this value as due to the systematics from the measurement.

Appendix 6.C Thermal Conductance Measurements with QP.4

The entire QP.4 chip we will use for these measurements is shown in Fig. 9, where we use the TES rectangles, as pictured in Fig. F.7 for convenience. We will measure thermal conductances of QP.4 in the following configurations: glued with GE-7031 varnish, resting on Cu and thermalized through the electronic wire bonds, and glued with rubber cement. We will also show the clean method of measuring GT​AG_{TA} via I​VIV curves at different bath temperatures. These TES rectangles have dimensions 800​μ​m×200​μ​m×40​nm800\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 200\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mathrm{nm}, 400​μ​m×100​μ​m×40​nm400\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 100\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mathrm{nm}, 200​μ​m×50​μ​m×40​nm200\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 50\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mathrm{nm} and 100​μ​m×25​μ​m×40​nm100\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 25\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mathrm{nm}, and will henceforth be referred to as TES800x200, TES400x100, TES200x50, and TES100x25, respectively. Each of the following measurements were done on a QP.4 chip from the same wafer, but each are different chips, thus giving variation on the various values of GT​AG_{TA} that we will measure for different TESs with the same rectangular dimensions.

1 GE-7031 Varnish

GE-7031 varnish is a common polymer-based adhesive for cryogenic applications. In our lab is has been frequently used to glue 1​cm21\,\mathrm{cm}^{2} substrates to our Cu housing. Because the GE-7031 varnish is dissimilar to the semiconductor substrate, just as the case with the cirlex clamps, the thermal conductance at the interface will be due to the mismatch of the elastic constants [95], giving an expected thermal conductance temperature dependence of G∝T3G\propto T^{3} (i.e. the power law exponent of the heat flow is expected to be n=4n=4). Practically, we have had some trouble in the past with the GE-7031 varnish thermal contraction being large enough that our 1​cm21\,\mathrm{cm}^{2} chips would frequently pop off of the Cu housing, and, depending on the device, the substrate may no longer have a good thermal connection to bath.

GA​BG_{AB} Measurement

To measure GA​BG_{AB}, we use TES200x50 as the heater and TES100x25 as the thermometer. In addition to the 5​m​Ω5\,\mathrm{m}\Omega shunt resistor, the normal resistance of TES200x50 in this measurement is 413​m​Ω413\,\mathrm{m}\Omega, with a parasitic resistance of 2.4​m​Ω2.4\,\mathrm{m}\Omega. The data from this measurement are reported in Table 5. The error in PA​BP_{AB} is set to be 10% of the measured power, based on an estimated 10% uncertainty in Rs​hR_{sh}. We fit Eq. (2) with nn allowed to be any value, and n=4n=4 fixed as expected from the phonon mismatch between the absorber and the GE-7031 varnish. In Fig. F.8, we show the results of these two fits and compare to the measured data, with the various fit parameters reported in Table 6.

GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

For the GT​AG_{TA} measurements with GE-7031 varnish, we used the quick measurement method with TES100x25 and TES200x50. The data from this measurement are reported in Tables 7 and 8, where the error in PT​AP_{TA} is estimated to be 10% of the measured power. Using Eq. (7), we can fit the power law with nn varying and n=5n=5 fixed, the latter as expected for a W TES. In Fig. F.9, we show the results of the fits as compared to the measured data, and report the various fit parameters in Table 9 for the two TESs.

2 Al Wire Bonds

To study a configuration without glue, we ran a set of rectangles where the thermalization of the chip was achieved through the superconducting Al wire bonds that are used for electrical readout. In this scenario, we do not expect to be the thermal conductance to be from an interface, but instead dominated by the lattice wave (phonon) contribution. Because Al has a critical temperature Tc=1.2​KT_{c}=1.2\,\mathrm{K}, and we are operating these TESs far below this value (tens of mK), the electrons have no contribution to the thermal transport due to being bound in Cooper pairs, and the thermal conductance is expected to be G∝T3G\propto T^{3} from the phonon contribution to the thermal transport (i.e. we expect n=4n=4 for the PA​BP_{AB} power law).

GA​BG_{AB} Measurement

To measure GA​BG_{AB}, we use TES200x50 as the heater and TES100x25 as the thermometer. In addition to the 5​m​Ω5\,\mathrm{m}\Omega shunt resistor, the normal resistance of TES200x50 in this measurement is 426​m​Ω426\,\mathrm{m}\Omega, with a parasitic resistance of 2.5​m​Ω2.5\,\mathrm{m}\Omega. The data from this measurement are reported in Table 10, where error in PA​BP_{AB} is set to be 10% of the measured power, based on an estimated 10% uncertainty in Rs​hR_{sh}. We then fit Eq. (2) with nn allowed to be any value, and n=4n=4 fixed as expected from the phonon contribution to the thermal conductance. In Fig. F.10, we show the results of these two fits and compare to the measured data, with the various fit parameters reported in Table 11.

GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

For the GT​AG_{TA} measurement, we use the quick measurement method for TES100x25 and TES200x50. The data from these measurements are reported in Tables 12 and 13, and the error in PT​AP_{TA} is estimated to be 10% of the measured power. Using Eq. (7), we fit the power law with nn varying and n=5n=5 fixed, the latter as expected for a W TES. In Fig. F.11, we show the results of the two fits as compared to the measured data, and report the various fit parameters in Table 14.

3 Rubber Cement

As the GE-7031 varnish had problems with glued chips popping off after cooling, it was recommended by Aritoki Suzuki that we try rubber cement (Elmer’s) as an alternative adhesive, as the Suzuki group had never experienced this in their lab. As with GE-7031 varnish and the cirlex clamps, rubber cement is dissimilar to the semiconductor substrate, and the thermal conductance at the interface will be due to the mismatch of the elastic constants [95], giving an expected thermal conductance temperature dependence of G∝T3G\propto T^{3}.

GA​BG_{AB} Measurement

In addition to the 5​m​Ω5\,\mathrm{m}\Omega shunt resistor, the normal resistance of TES200x50 in this measurement is 423​m​Ω423\,\mathrm{m}\Omega, with a parasitic resistance of 4.3​m​Ω4.3\,\mathrm{m}\Omega. The data from this measurement are reported in Table 15. The error in PA​BP_{AB} is set to be 10% of the measured power, based on an estimated 10% uncertainty in Rs​hR_{sh}. We then fit Eq. (2) with nn allowed to be any value, and n=4n=4 fixed as expected from the phonon mismatch between the absorber and the rubber cement. In Fig. F.12, we show the results of these two fits and compare to the measured data, with the various fit parameters reported in Table 16.

For each of the previous sections, we showed examples of the quick GT​AG_{TA} measurement method, which is fast, but could be subject to systematic errors as noted in the explanation of the method. In this section, we show examples of clean GT​AG_{TA} measurements via IV sweeps at various bath temperatures for TES800x200, TES400x100, and TES200x50.

GT​AG_{TA} Measurement

Note that we chose an operating resistance of R0=150​m​ΩR_{0}=150\,\mathrm{m}\Omega and interpolated between data points to ensure estimate the bias power of the TES at this value. In Fig. F.16, we show the detector setup from one of our runs in the dilution refrigerator at UC Berkeley, where we will use the 4% detector with disconnected fins to measure the thermal conductance from absorber to bath of the gold pad. Both of these chips are resting on the gold-plated Cu plate, and each has a TES rectangle of dimensions 295​μ​m×40​μ​m×40​nm295\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 40\,\mathrm{nm}, henceforth referred to as TES295x40. Because the TES rectangle on the connected fin device had a short, we used the disconnected fin device instead.

1 Au Pad

On the Si substrate of the detector, a gold pad was deposited with dimensions 300​μ​m×300​μ​m×750​nm300\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 300\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times 750\,\mathrm{nm} for the purpose of thermalization through a gold wire. The sizing of the pad was decided by C. W. Fink, and we will use it as a data point for the thermal conductance of a thin gold film. As noted in Refs. [225, 226], the power law exponent for a thin gold film can be expected to be either n=5n=5 for an ordered metal [227, 94, 228], or n=6n=6 for a disordered metal [229, 230].

GA​BG_{AB} Measurement

To measure GA​BG_{AB}, we use TES295x40 as the heater and array of disconnected fin QETs as the thermometer. In addition to the 5​m​Ω5\,\mathrm{m}\Omega shunt resistor, the normal resistance of TES295x40 in this measurement is 344​m​Ω344\,\mathrm{m}\Omega, with a parasitic resistance of 2.6​m​Ω2.6\,\mathrm{m}\Omega. We then fit Eq. (2) with nn allowed to be any value, and n=5n=5 and n=6n=6 fixed as expected from ordered and disordered metals, respectively. In Fig. F.17, we show the results of these fits and compare to the measured data, with the various fit parameters reported in Table 19. Both n=5n=5 and n=6n=6 seem to reasonably describe the power law, so we do not make a claim as to which is correct, but instead report the values for both.

Appendix 6.E Summary of Measurements

In this appendix, we discussed methods for measuring the thermal conductances from TES to absorber and absorber to bath and used the methods for a variety of different measurements, where the substrate holding scheme varied significantly. The various values from that we fit are summarized in Table 20 for the GA​BG_{AB} fits and Table 21 for the GT​AG_{TA} fits.

For the Σe​p\Sigma_{ep} values, previous measurements have seen Σe​p,Au=2.4​GW/(K5​m3)\Sigma_{ep,\,\mathrm{Au}}=2.4\,\mathrm{GW}/(\mathrm{K}^{5}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}) [231] and Σe​p,W=0.3​GW/(K5​m3)\Sigma_{ep,\,\mathrm{W}}=0.3\,\mathrm{GW}/(\mathrm{K}^{5}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}) [232] for Au and W, respectively. Our measurements for W are completely consistent with that value, while the n=5n=5 value for Au is a factor of 5 smaller than previously measured. It is unknown why this is the case. For the n=6n=6 power law for Au (i.e. a disordered film), it has been measured as Σe​p,Au′=60​GW/(K6​m3)\Sigma^{\prime}_{ep,\,\mathrm{Au}}=60\,\mathrm{GW}/(\mathrm{K}^{6}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}) [225, 226], a value which itself depends on the level of disorder. If this were the case, then the n=6n=6 value we measured is a factor of 6 lower, which would imply that the level of disorder is different for our film (i.e. less disordered). This could be the case, as our Au film is about a factor of 10 thicker (750​nm750\,\mathrm{nm} vs. 57​nm57\,\mathrm{nm}), and the boundary scattering effects would be smaller. Another possibility could be that the Au pad itself is not well-connected to the substrate, such that there is an extra interfacial thermal resistance that we cannot measure. More thermal conductance measurements of the Au pad system would be useful to understand the difference.

Chapter 7 Reduction of Vibrational Noise

The decoupling of sensitive detectors or instruments from environmental vibrations has been pursued by many cryogenic experiments, usually using a three-dimensional elastic pendulum [208] for passive vibration isolation [209, 210, 211, 212, 213, 214, 215]. These vibrations can provide additional in the experimental, reducing sensitivity of an experiment. This is especially important in rare event searches that work towards the lowest possible noise environments. For the CPD studied in the main body of this thesis, the excess signals observed within the DM ROI could removed with a stress-free holding scheme, which would then be sensitive to vibrations, thus motivating the design and fabrication of an internal vibration decoupler. A common source of vibrations in cryogenic experiments that use a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator is the pulse-tube cryocooler. The pulse-tube cryocooler (PT) is critical to achieve sub-10​mK10\,\mathrm{mK} base temperatures and relies on a oscillating compression system to provide cooling power for the dilution refrigerator. The operating frequency of these oscillations is low, with 1.4​Hz1.4\,\mathrm{Hz} as a common frequency. Thus, the goal is to have a system that works as a low-pass filter with a fundamental frequency that is as low as possible. Practically, this will be constrained by the dilution refrigerator dimensions, as we will discuss later in this appendix.

For the system used in the Pyle Lab, we expand upon the designs of two different vibration isolation systems: one developed by R. Maisonobe et al. [209] and one developed by L. Gottardi et al. [210]. We will call each of these vibration decouplers the “Maisonobe system” and the “Gottardi system,” respectively.

As shown in Fig. G.1, the Maisonobe system is based on a single elastic pendulum placed in the center of the cryostat plate. Their design is simple—they use a single spring pendulum from the 1​K1\,\mathrm{K} to 10​mK10\,\mathrm{mK} stage. The pendulum ultimately giving the best performance is based on a nylon wire and a single stainless steel spring, together giving fundamental frequencies of 1.8​Hz1.8\,\mathrm{Hz} in the vertical direction and 0.8​Hz0.8\,\mathrm{Hz} in the radial direction. This system allowed the detectors studied to achieve baseline energy resolutions between a factor 2–40 better than without any vibration decoupling.

The Gottardi system is based on the taber vibration isolator proposed in Ref. [211]. This system uses a kevlar wire which is clamped in a triangular configuration, as shown in Fig. G.2, which effectively acts as three springs symmetrically placed at 120∘120^{\circ} intervals. This allows the design to attenuate vibrations along more degrees of freedom than the Maisonobe system. The design also has two stages, as opposed to one, which increases the attenuation power above the fundamental frequencies with the cost of increasing them by a small amount (as opposed to a one-stage system). For their system, the fundamental frequencies were shown to be on the order of tens of Hz. When adjusting this design to the approximate dimensions of the Pyle Lab fridge it was found that the highest frequencies were still about 10 Hz, thus we decided not to use this design.

For the Pyle Lab, we considered a model similar to as depicted in Fig. G.3. This system can be thought of as an in-between for both the Maisonobe [209] and Gottardi [210] systems. With the springs, we should be able to achieve lower fundamental frequencies with the system (as well as in a two-stage version), as well as have attenuation along more degrees of freedom than the Maisonobe system. In order to understand the expected fundamental frequencies in this proposed system, we will derive them using Lagrangian mechanics.

Appendix 7.A Derivation of Fundamental Frequencies

In deriving the fundamental frequencies of the vibration decoupler, we will consider to versions of our design: one with a single vibrational stage, and one with two vibrational stages.

1 One Stage

The one-stage derivation is as follows. First, we calculate the equilibrium state with the usual sum of forces

−m​g+3​k​(le​q−l0)=0,-mg+3k\left(l_{eq}-l_{0}\right)=0\,, (1)

where we assume that the system is such that the center of mass is at the disk’s center. If we compare to the Maisonobe system, we see that the change in length of each spring will be a third of that in the Maisonobe system, assuming the same spring constants.

In order to describe how the lengths of the springs change under various movements of the disk, we need to first define the coordinate system. Specifically, we will set the origin of the coordinate system as the center of the tops of the three springs. In other words, the center-of-mass of the disk at equilibrium is set to be

𝐱c​m=x​𝐱^+y​𝐲^+(z−le​q)​𝐳^,\mathbf{x}_{cm}=x{\bm{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}+y{\bm{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}+(z-l_{eq}){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{z}}}}\,, (2)

where le​ql_{eq} is the equilibrium length of the springs. We also define the xx-axis as some angle θ\theta from spring 1, such that spring 2 and spring 3 are placed θ+2​π3\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3} and θ+4​π3\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3} away from the xx-axis. In other words, we define the horizontal axes to be arbitrary. Using our coordinate system, the locations of the top of the three springs are defined as

𝐑1\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{1} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ)​𝐲^],\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}+\sin\left(\theta\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}\right]\,, (3)
𝐑2\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{2} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ+2​π3)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ+2​π3)​𝐲^],\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}\right]\,, (4)
𝐑3\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{3} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ+4​π3)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ+4​π3)​𝐲^].\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right){\bm{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}\right]\,. (5)

In order to find the vector of each spring, we can follow the vector path of the top of a spring 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i}, to the origin, to the location of the center-of-mass (including its displacement), to the bottom of the spring (with some rotation of the disk). Thus, for spring ii, its vector is

𝐥i=𝐱c​m+𝐑i′−𝐑i,\mathbf{l}_{i}=\mathbf{x}_{cm}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{i}\,, (6)

where 𝐑i′\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i} is the rotated 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i}.

Because the three springs are placed on the edges of the disk, we expect six degrees of freedom, also seen in the Gottardi system. There will be three translational and three rotational modes. The most general way to calculate the fundamental frequencies of these modes would be to take into account all possible rotations of the disk. However, this quickly becomes a mess of Euler angles and is unwieldy to do by hand.

Thus, to simply our efforts, we will first calculate the modes of the system when we allow rotations of the disk about the horizontal axis, and then calculate the modes of the system when we allow rotations of the disk about the vertical axis. We note that there is an assumption here that the horizontal rotational modes and vertical rotational modes do not couple, which should be a good assumption simply based on intuition of the system.

Rotations about the horizontal—To find all of the fundamental frequencies of the system when allowing for rotations about the horizontal, we will begin by defining the kinetic energy, potential energy, and Lagrangian equations as

T\displaystyle T =12​m​(x˙2+y˙2+z˙2)+12​Ix​ϕ˙2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}+\dot{z}^{2})+\frac{1}{2}I_{x}\dot{\phi}^{2}, (7)
V\displaystyle V =∑i=13[12​k​(li−l0)2]+m​g​z,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\left[\frac{1}{2}k(l_{i}-l_{0})^{2}\right]+mgz, (8)
L\displaystyle L =T−V.\displaystyle=T-V. (9)

The lil_{i} terms are nonlinear, so the Euler-Lagrange equations that we would get out of this Lagrangian would not be analytically solvable. However, we can Taylor expand the potential energy around the equilibrium point to second order to estimate the natural frequencies for small oscillations. As we are looking at rotations of the disk about the horizontal by some angle ϕ\phi, we can relate 𝐑i′\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i} to 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i} by

𝐑i′=[1000cos⁡ϕ−sin⁡ϕ0sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ]​𝐑i.\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&\cos{\phi}&-\sin{\phi}\\ 0&\sin{\phi}&\cos{\phi}\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_{i}. (10)

For the zeroth order term of the Taylor expansion, the potential energy is simply V0=32​k​(le​q−l0)2V_{0}=\frac{3}{2}k(l_{eq}-l_{0})^{2}, which is the potential energy stored in each spring at equilibrium. For the first order terms, it can be shown that the first derivative of the potential energy with respect to each variable is zero when evaluated at equilibrium (the point at which we are expanding). For the second order terms, it can be shown that the cross-terms all evaluate to zero at equilibrium, while the second derivatives with respect to each variable are nonzero. Specifically, the potential energy can be approximated as

V≈\displaystyle V\approx V0+32​k​(1−l0le​q)​x2+32​k​(1−l0le​q)​y2\displaystyle V_{0}+\frac{3}{2}k\left(1-\frac{l_{0}}{l_{eq}}\right)x^{2}+\frac{3}{2}k\left(1-\frac{l_{0}}{l_{eq}}\right)y^{2}
+32​k​z2+34​k​R2​ϕ2.\displaystyle+\frac{3}{2}kz^{2}+\frac{3}{4}kR^{2}\phi^{2}. (11)

Using our equilibrium relation, we can simplify this to

V≈\displaystyle V\approx V0+12​m​gle​q​x2+12​m​gle​q​y2+32​k​z2+34​k​R2​ϕ2.\displaystyle V_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mg}{l_{eq}}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mg}{l_{eq}}y^{2}+\frac{3}{2}kz^{2}+\frac{3}{4}kR^{2}\phi^{2}. (12)

It is clear that the Euler-Lagrange equations will completely decouple, and we do not have any mixing of modes when Taylor expanding up to second order. Applying the Euler-Lagrange equations, we find that the decoupled equations of motion are

x¨+gle​q​x\displaystyle\ddot{x}+\frac{g}{l_{eq}}x =0,\displaystyle=0, (13)
y¨+gle​q​y\displaystyle\ddot{y}+\frac{g}{l_{eq}}y =0,\displaystyle=0, (14)
z¨+3​km​z\displaystyle\ddot{z}+\frac{3k}{m}z =0,\displaystyle=0, (15)
ϕ¨+3​k​R22​Ix​ϕ\displaystyle\ddot{\phi}+\frac{3kR^{2}}{2I_{x}}\phi =0.\displaystyle=0. (16)

Thus, we have that the fundamental frequencies are

fx,y\displaystyle f_{x,y} =12​π​gle​q,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{l_{eq}}}, (17)
fz\displaystyle f_{z} =12​π​3​km,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{3k}{m}}, (18)
fx,y,r​o​t.\displaystyle f_{x,y,rot.} =12​π​3​k​R22​Ix.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{3kR^{2}}{2I_{x}}}. (19)

Note that the xx and yy translational modes have the same fundamental frequencies due to the symmetry of system. Because we set up the system to have arbitrary xx and yy axes, the fundamental frequencies about the xx and yy axes are identical as well.

Rotations about the vertical—To find all of the fundamental frequencies of the system when allowing for rotations about the vertical by some angle ψ\psi, we will again define the kinetic energy, potential energy, and Lagrangian equations as

T\displaystyle T =12​m​(x˙2+y˙2+z˙2)+12​Iz​ψ˙2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}+\dot{z}^{2})+\frac{1}{2}I_{z}\dot{\psi}^{2}, (20)
V\displaystyle V =∑i=13[12​k​(li−l0)2]+m​g​z,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\left[\frac{1}{2}k(l_{i}-l_{0})^{2}\right]+mgz, (21)
L\displaystyle L =T−V.\displaystyle=T-V. (22)

We will again Taylor expand the potential energy, where the relation between 𝐑i′\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i} and 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i} is instead

𝐑i′=[cos⁡ψ−sin⁡ψ0sin⁡ψcos⁡ψ0001]​𝐑i.\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\psi}&-\sin{\psi}&0\\ \sin{\psi}&\cos{\psi}&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_{i}. (23)

For the zeroth order term of the Taylor expansion, the potential energy is again V0=32​k​(le​q−l0)2V_{0}=\frac{3}{2}k(l_{eq}-l_{0})^{2}, as expected. For the first order terms, it can be shown that the first derivative of the potential energy with respect to each variable is zero when evaluated at equilibrium. For the second order terms, it can be shown that the cross-terms all evaluate to zero at equilibrium, while the second derivatives with respect to each variable are nonzero. Specifically, the potential energy can be approximated as

V≈\displaystyle V\approx V0+32​k​(1−l0le​q)​x2+32​k​(1−l0le​q)​y2\displaystyle V_{0}+\frac{3}{2}k\left(1-\frac{l_{0}}{l_{eq}}\right)x^{2}+\frac{3}{2}k\left(1-\frac{l_{0}}{l_{eq}}\right)y^{2}
+32​k​z2+32​k​(1−l0le​q)​R2​ψ2.\displaystyle+\frac{3}{2}kz^{2}+\frac{3}{2}k\left(1-\frac{l_{0}}{l_{eq}}\right)R^{2}\psi^{2}. (24)

Using our equilibrium relation, we can simplify this to

V≈\displaystyle V\approx V0+12​m​gle​q​x2+12​m​gle​q​y2+32​k​z2+12​m​g​R2le​q​ψ2.\displaystyle V_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mg}{l_{eq}}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mg}{l_{eq}}y^{2}+\frac{3}{2}kz^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mgR^{2}}{l_{eq}}\psi^{2}. (25)

We again have that the Euler-Lagrange equations will completely decouple, and we do not have any mixing of modes when Taylor expanding up to second order. Applying the Euler-Lagrange equations, we find that the decoupled equations of motion are

x¨+gle​q​x\displaystyle\ddot{x}+\frac{g}{l_{eq}}x =0,\displaystyle=0, (26)
y¨+gle​q​y\displaystyle\ddot{y}+\frac{g}{l_{eq}}y =0,\displaystyle=0, (27)
z¨+3​km​z\displaystyle\ddot{z}+\frac{3k}{m}z =0,\displaystyle=0, (28)
ψ¨+m​g​R2Iz​le​q​ψ\displaystyle\ddot{\psi}+\frac{mgR^{2}}{I_{z}l_{eq}}\psi =0.\displaystyle=0. (29)

Thus, the translational modes match those that we derived for when studying the system under horizontal rotations. Thus, we can summarize all of the different fundamental frequencies as

fx,y\displaystyle f_{x,y} =12​π​gle​q,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{l_{eq}}}, (30)
fz\displaystyle f_{z} =12​π​3​km,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{3k}{m}}, (31)
fx,y,r​o​t.\displaystyle f_{x,y,rot.} =12​π​3​k​R22​Ix,y,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{3kR^{2}}{2I_{x,y}}}, (32)
fz,r​o​t.\displaystyle f_{z,rot.} =12​π​m​g​R2Iz​le​q,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{mgR^{2}}{I_{z}l_{eq}}}, (33)

where fz,r​o​t.f_{z,rot.} follows from solving the differential equation describing ψ\psi.

Thus, we have that, using the Taylor expansion of the potential energy, we can analytically solve the system using the Lagrangian formalism. The next Pyle Lab setup to study will be the two-stage vibration decoupler.

2 Two Stages

As opposed to the derivation of the one-stage system, we will instead go through the various intuitive vibrational modes for the two-stage system case by case. This simplifies the derivation as we are now assuming that the modes decouple, rather than proving this by checking all of the various derivatives. We will also assume that the spring constants for each spring within a stage are the same, but different between the two stages, that the springs for the two stages have different equilibrium lengths, and that the masses of the two stages are also different (but the same disk radius). In Fig. G.4, we show the proposed system, as well as define the coordinate system used.

Case 1—Let’s start with vertical translations of the two-stage system. The kinetic energy, potential energy, and Lagrangian can be written as:

T=\displaystyle T= 12​m1​z˙12+12​m2​z˙22,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}m_{1}\dot{z}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m_{2}\dot{z}_{2}^{2}, (34)
V=\displaystyle V= 32​k1​z12+32​k2​(z2−z1)2+m1​g​z1+m2​g​z2,\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}k_{1}z_{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}k_{2}(z_{2}-z_{1})^{2}+m_{1}gz_{1}+m_{2}gz_{2}, (35)
L=\displaystyle L= 12​m1​z˙12+12​m2​z˙22−32​k1​z12−32​k2​(z2−z1)2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}m_{1}\dot{z}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m_{2}\dot{z}_{2}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}k_{1}z_{1}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}k_{2}(z_{2}-z_{1})^{2}
−m1​g​z1−m2​g​z2,\displaystyle-m_{1}gz_{1}-m_{2}gz_{2}, (36)

where each spring in a stage has identical potential energies (hence the factors of 3). After carrying out the Euler-Lagrange equations and simplifying, we have two coupled differential equations:

m1​z¨1+3​(k1+k2)​z1−3​k2​z2\displaystyle m_{1}\ddot{z}_{1}+3(k_{1}+k_{2})z_{1}-3k_{2}z_{2} =0,\displaystyle=0, (37)
mz​z¨2−3​k2​z1+3​k2​z2\displaystyle m_{z}\ddot{z}_{2}-3k_{2}z_{1}+3k_{2}z_{2} =0,\displaystyle=0, (38)

where we have again neglected constant values (as they can be removed by a change in coordinate system). After solving this system for the eigenvalues, we have that the natural frequencies are

ω2=\displaystyle\omega^{2}= 3​[(k1+k2)​m2+k2​m1]2​m1​m2​{1±1−4​m1​m2​k1​k2[(k1+k2)​m2+k2​m1]2}.\displaystyle\frac{3[(k_{1}+k_{2})m_{2}+k_{2}m_{1}]}{2m_{1}m_{2}}\left\{1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{1}m_{2}k_{1}k_{2}}{[(k_{1}+k_{2})m_{2}+k_{2}m_{1}]^{2}}}\right\}. (39)

Case 2—Next, let’s look at horizontal translations of the disks. This can be thought of as the double pendulum modes for the disks’ centers of mass. We start by showing the kinetic and potential energy equations in xx and yy coordinates:

T=\displaystyle T= 12​m1​(x˙1+y˙1)2+12​m2​(x˙2+y˙2)2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}m_{1}\left(\dot{x}_{1}+\dot{y}_{1}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m_{2}\left(\dot{x}_{2}+\dot{y}_{2}\right)^{2}, (40)
V=\displaystyle V= m1​g​y1+m2​g​y2.\displaystyle m_{1}gy_{1}+m_{2}gy_{2}. (41)

Since this will be oscillations due to the angles that the disk centers of mass make with the vertical, we need to change our variables to be in terms of these angles for each center of mass (α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}). That is, we have that

x1\displaystyle x_{1} =l1sinα1,\displaystyle=l_{1}\sin\alpha_{1}, (42)
x1˙\displaystyle\dot{x_{1}} =l1α˙1cosα1,\displaystyle=l_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}\cos\alpha_{1}, (43)
y1\displaystyle y_{1} =−l1cosα1,\displaystyle=-l_{1}\cos\alpha_{1}, (44)
y˙1\displaystyle\dot{y}_{1} =l1α˙1sinα1,\displaystyle=l_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}\sin\alpha_{1}, (45)
x2\displaystyle x_{2} =l1sinα1+l2sinα2,\displaystyle=l_{1}\sin\alpha_{1}+l_{2}\sin\alpha_{2}, (46)
x2˙\displaystyle\dot{x_{2}} =l1α˙1cosα1+l2α˙2cosα2,\displaystyle=l_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}\cos\alpha_{1}+l_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{2}\cos\alpha_{2}, (47)
y2\displaystyle y_{2} =−l1cosα1−l2cosα2,\displaystyle=-l_{1}\cos\alpha_{1}-l_{2}\cos\alpha_{2}, (48)
y˙2\displaystyle\dot{y}_{2} =l1α˙1sinα1+l2α˙2sinα2.\displaystyle=l_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}\sin\alpha_{1}+l_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{2}\sin\alpha_{2}. (49)

We can plug all of these relations into the kinetic and potential energy equations, which gives us

T=\displaystyle T= 12​(m1+m2)​l12​α˙12\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})l_{1}^{2}\dot{\alpha}_{1}^{2}
+m2​l1​l2​α˙1​α˙2​cos⁡(α1−α2)+12​m2​l2​α˙22,\displaystyle+m_{2}l_{1}l_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{2}\cos(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})+\frac{1}{2}m_{2}l_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{2}^{2}, (50)
V=\displaystyle V= −(m1+m2)gl1cosα1−m2gl2cosα2.\displaystyle-(m_{1}+m_{2})gl_{1}\cos\alpha_{1}-m_{2}gl_{2}\cos\alpha_{2}. (51)

Using the Euler-Lagrange equations and the small angle approximation, one can find that this gives us two coupled differential equations:

(m1+m2)​l12​α¨1+m2​l1​l2​α¨2+(m1+m2)​g​l1​α1\displaystyle(m_{1}+m_{2})l_{1}^{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{1}+m_{2}l_{1}l_{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{2}+(m_{1}+m_{2})gl_{1}\alpha_{1} =0,\displaystyle=0, (52)
m2​l22​α¨2+m2​l1​l2​α¨1+m2​g​l2​α2\displaystyle m_{2}l_{2}^{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{2}+m_{2}l_{1}l_{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{1}+m_{2}gl_{2}\alpha_{2} =0.\displaystyle=0. (53)

After solving this system of equations for the eigenfrequencies, we have that the natural frequencies are

ω2=\displaystyle\omega^{2}= (m1+m2)​(l1+l2)​g2​m1​l1​l2​{1±1−4​m1​l1​l2(m1+m2)​(l1+l2)2}.\displaystyle\frac{(m_{1}+m_{2})(l_{1}+l_{2})g}{2m_{1}l_{1}l_{2}}\left\{1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{1}l_{1}l_{2}}{(m_{1}+m_{2})(l_{1}+l_{2})^{2}}}\right\}. (54)

Case 3—Next, we look at the eigenmodes for rotations about a horizontal axis, where each disk rotates by an angle of α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, respectively. This is shown in Fig. G.5 In this case, we will need to keep track of the locations of the springs along the disk, remembering that each spring is vertically aligned. In this case, we again remind the reader of the below relations for each of the spring locations, where the same holds true for each stage.

𝐑1\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{1} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ)​𝐲^],\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta\right)\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\sin\left(\theta\right)\hat{\mathbf{y}}\right]\,, (55)
𝐑2\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{2} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ+2​π3)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ+2​π3)​𝐲^],\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat{\mathbf{y}}\right]\,, (56)
𝐑3\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{3} =R⁡[cos⁡(θ+4​π3)​𝐱^+sin⁡(θ+4​π3)​𝐲^].\displaystyle=R\left[\cos\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\hat{\mathbf{y}}\right]\,. (57)

Thus, we can write the unsimplified version of the kinetic and potential energy equations:

T=\displaystyle T= 12​I1​α˙12+12​I2​α˙22,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}I_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{2}^{2}, (58)
V=\displaystyle V= 12k1[(Rcos(θ)sin(α1)]2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}k_{1}[(R\cos(\theta)\sin(\alpha_{1})]^{2}
+12​k1​[R​cos⁡(θ+2​π3)​sin⁡(α1)]2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}k_{1}\left[R\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\sin(\alpha_{1})\right]^{2}
+12​k1​[R​cos⁡(θ+4​π3)​sin⁡(α1)]2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}k_{1}\left[R\cos\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\sin(\alpha_{1})\right]^{2}.
+12​k2​{R​cos⁡(θ)​[sin⁡(α1)−sin⁡(α2)]}2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}k_{2}\{R\cos(\theta)[\sin(\alpha_{1})-\sin(\alpha_{2})]\}^{2} (59)
+12​k2​{R​cos⁡(θ+2​π3)​[sin⁡(α1)−sin⁡(α2)]}2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}k_{2}\left\{R\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)[\sin(\alpha_{1})-\sin(\alpha_{2})]\right\}^{2}
+12​k2​{R​cos⁡(θ+4​π3)​[sin⁡(α1)−sin⁡(α2)]}2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}k_{2}\left\{R\cos\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)[\sin(\alpha_{1})-\sin(\alpha_{2})]\right\}^{2}.

Using angle-addition formulae and some algebra, we find that the potential energy equation simplifies to:

V=\displaystyle V= 34​(k1+k2)​R2​sin2⁡α1\displaystyle\frac{3}{4}(k_{1}+k_{2})R^{2}\sin^{2}\alpha_{1}
−32k2R2sinα1sinα2\displaystyle-\frac{3}{2}k_{2}R^{2}\sin\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{2} (60)
+34​k2​R2​sin2⁡α2.\displaystyle+\frac{3}{4}k_{2}R^{2}\sin^{2}\alpha_{2}.

We note that, as expected, there is no dependence on the coordinate system used. Now, we can use the Euler-Lagrange equations and the small-angle approximation to find the coupled differential equations.

I1​α¨1+32​(k1+k2)​R2​α1−32​k2​R2​α2\displaystyle I_{1}\ddot{\alpha}_{1}+\frac{3}{2}(k_{1}+k_{2})R^{2}\alpha_{1}-\frac{3}{2}k_{2}R^{2}\alpha_{2} =0,\displaystyle=0, (61)
I2​α¨2−32​k2​R2​α1+32​k2​R2​α2\displaystyle I_{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{2}-\frac{3}{2}k_{2}R^{2}\alpha_{1}+\frac{3}{2}k_{2}R^{2}\alpha_{2} =0.\displaystyle=0. (62)

Solving for the eigenfrequencies, we find that

ω2=\displaystyle\omega^{2}= 3​R2​[(k1+k2)​I2+k2​I1]4​I1​I2​{1±1−4​I1​I2​k1​k2[(k1+k2)​I2+k2​I1]2}.\displaystyle\frac{3R^{2}[(k_{1}+k_{2})I_{2}+k_{2}I_{1}]}{4I_{1}I_{2}}\left\{1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4I_{1}I_{2}k_{1}k_{2}}{[(k_{1}+k_{2})I_{2}+k_{2}I_{1}]^{2}}}\right\}. (63)

Case 4—Lastly, we look at the natural frequencies for rotations of the disks about the vertical axis, i.e. the double torsion pendulum modes. In this case, we will say that each disk rotates about the vertical by angles α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, respectively. In Fig. G.6, we show an example of this type of rotation. We note that in this case, each spring is rotated by an angle θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} with respect to the vertical. Thus, the kinetic energy and potential energy equations are:

T\displaystyle T =12​I1​α˙12+12​I2​α˙22,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}I_{1}\dot{\alpha}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I_{2}\dot{\alpha}_{2}^{2}, (64)
V\displaystyle V =−(m1+m2)gl1cosθ1−m2gl2cosθ2,\displaystyle=-(m_{1}+m_{2})gl_{1}\cos\theta_{1}-m_{2}gl_{2}\cos\theta_{2}, (65)

where we have dropped the constants in the potential energy and neglected the kinetic energy due to vertical movement, as this is very small (also the equations are no longer analytically solvable).

Now, we have that the angles θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} are related to the α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} by the following relations:

l1​θ1\displaystyle l_{1}\theta_{1} =R​α1,\displaystyle=R\alpha_{1}, (66)
l1​θ1+l2​θ2\displaystyle l_{1}\theta_{1}+l_{2}\theta_{2} =R​α2.\displaystyle=R\alpha_{2}. (67)

Next, we carry out the Euler-Lagrange equations, use the small-angle approximation, and use the above relations to arrive at our coupled differential equations:

I1​α¨1+(m1+m2l1+m2l2)​g​R2​α1−m2l2​g​R2​α2\displaystyle I_{1}\ddot{\alpha}_{1}+\left(\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}}{l_{1}}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}\right)gR^{2}\alpha_{1}-\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}gR^{2}\alpha_{2} =0,\displaystyle=0, (68)
I2​α¨2−m2l2​g​R2​α1+m2l2​g​R2​α2\displaystyle I_{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{2}-\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}gR^{2}\alpha_{1}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}gR^{2}\alpha_{2} =0.\displaystyle=0. (69)

Solving for the eigenfrequencies, we find that

ω2=\displaystyle\omega^{2}= [(m1+m2l1+m2l2)​I2+m2l2​I1]​g​R22​I1​I2​{1±1−4​I1​I2​m1+m2l1​m2l2[(m1+m2l1+m2l2)​I2+m2l2​I1]2}.\displaystyle\frac{\left[\left(\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}}{l_{1}}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}\right)I_{2}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}I_{1}\right]gR^{2}}{2I_{1}I_{2}}\left\{1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4I_{1}I_{2}\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}}{l_{1}}\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}}{\left[\left(\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}}{l_{1}}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}\right)I_{2}+\frac{m_{2}}{l_{2}}I_{1}\right]^{2}}}\right\}. (70)

3 Spring Mode Intuition

We can gain some intuition on the final vibrational system via these fundamental frequencies. First, we note that the frequencies follow two basic forms: pendulum frequencies (i.e. f∼g/lf\sim\sqrt{g/l}) and spring frequencies (i.e. f∼k/mf\sim\sqrt{k/m}). Thus, we have that the ideal system will have springs that have the smallest spring rates and pendula that are as long as possible. These will be limited by the design constraints of our system, as will be discussed in Section 2.

However, one constraint that we can use to quickly gain intuition on our spring design is that we have a finite vertical volume for our system. For the one-stage system, we should use the full vertical volume. For the two-stage system, this means that the two stretched lengths must add up to some maximum value that is defined by the dilution refrigerator geometry. For our system, we will see that 0.5​m0.5\,\mathrm{m} is roughly this maximum. If we take this constraint, we can see from Fig. G.7 that a representative pendulum mode for the two-stage system will have its lowest value with the first stage and second stage springs having the same length.

It is also worth discussing mass distribution between the two stages. For the one-stage system, it is simple, as the spring modes imply to have the single stage be as heavy as possible. For the two-stage system, it will be more complex, as we need to know how to distribute the mass between stages. To do this, we will assume some total mass of 15​kg15\,\mathrm{kg} as a placeholder value for that of the system. In Fig. G.8, we see that a characteristic pendulum mode implies that as much mass as possible should be placed on the upper stage. On the other hand, if we look at a characteristic spring mode, then we see that there will be an upper bound on this value (depending on the spring constants), as shown in Fig. G.9. Nonetheless, the inequality that m1>m2m_{1}>m_{2}, or that the upper stage should have more mass than the lower stage, will hold. Thus, we will design our system with the intuition that we should put more mass on the upper stage than on the lower stage and make a decision on the distribution based on the spring constants we will be able to use.

Appendix 7.B Extension Spring Design

We have our expected fundamental frequencies and a small amount on intuition for some of the two-stage system’s values. With this in mind, we need to understand some of the fundamental constraints of our system. That is, we must know what the geometric constraints of the dilution refrigerator are (e.g. the maximum vertical space, the horizontal space), as well as constraints on spring design from an engineering point-of-view.

1 Design Principles

For spring design, the majority of the equations and rules are well-known in standard mechanical engineering textbooks, such as Shigley’s Mechanical Engineering Design [233], which we will follow when designing our springs.

Spring Rate

We start with the maximum stress in a wire being a superposition of the direct shear stress and the torsional shear stress:

τmax=FA+T​rJ,\tau_{\mathrm{max}}=\frac{F}{A}+\frac{Tr}{J}, (71)

where FF is the applied force, AA is the cross sectional area of the wire, TT is the applied torque, rr is the radius of the coiled wire, and JJ is the polar moment of area. To relate these values directly to the dimensions of the spring, we have that

T\displaystyle T =12​F​D,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}FD, (72)
r\displaystyle r =d2,\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2}, (73)
J\displaystyle J =π​d432,\displaystyle=\frac{\pi d^{4}}{32}, (74)
A\displaystyle A =π​d24,\displaystyle=\frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}, (75)

where DD is the average spring diameter, and dd is the wire diameter. Each of these values are shown diagrammatically in Fig. G.10.

Plugging these values in Eq. (71), we have that

τmax=8​F​Dπ​d3+4​F​πd2,\tau_{\mathrm{max}}=\frac{8FD}{\pi d^{3}}+\frac{4F\pi}{d^{2}}, (76)

which can be further simplified with the definition of the spring index C≡D/dC\equiv D/d and the shear stress-correction factor Ks≡2​C+12​CK_{s}\equiv\frac{2C+1}{2C}, giving

τmax=Ks​8​F​Dπ​d3.\tau_{\mathrm{max}}=K_{s}\frac{8FD}{\pi d^{3}}. (77)

However, this shear stress-correction factor relies on the assumption that the wire is straight, which of course is not true for a spring. Note that a general engineering rule-of-thumb for spring design is that CC should fall in the range of 4<C<124<C<12, as a spring with index outside of this range will be prone to failure. Generally, in order to be conservative by using the largest empirical stress-correction factor, it is common to replace KsK_{s} with the Bergsträsser factor

KB≡4​C+24​C−3,K_{B}\equiv\frac{4C+2}{4C-3}, (78)

which will be larger for a given CC, as compared to KsK_{s}. Thus, this gives maximum stress of

τmax=KB​8​F​Dπ​d3.\tau_{\mathrm{max}}=K_{B}\frac{8FD}{\pi d^{3}}. (79)

At this point, it is of importance for us to relate the total deflection of the spring yy to the force FF. As shown again in Ref. [233], Castigliano’s theorem will result in

y=8​F​D3​Nad4​G,y=\frac{8FD^{3}N_{a}}{d^{4}G}, (80)

where GG is the modulus of rigidity of the spring material, and NaN_{a} is the number of active coils (we will define number of active coils in the following paragraphs). Thus, we know that the spring constant is (via Hooke’s Law) defined by the ratio of the force to the spring deflection (k=F/yk=F/y), which gives for a spring that

k=d4​G8​D3​Na.k=\frac{d^{4}G}{8D^{3}N_{a}}. (81)
Adding Hooks

The maximum tensile stress at AA in Fig. G.11 is given by

σA=F⁡[(K)A​16​Dπ​d3+4π​d2],\sigma_{A}=F\left[(K)_{A}\frac{16D}{\pi d^{3}}+\frac{4}{\pi d^{2}}\right], (82)

where (K)A(K)_{A} is a bending stress-correction factor for curvature

(K)A=4​C12−C1−14​C1​(C1−1)(K)_{A}=\frac{4C_{1}^{2}-C_{1}-1}{4C_{1}(C_{1}-1)} (83)

and

C1=2​r1d.C_{1}=\frac{2r_{1}}{d}. (84)

The maximum torsional stress at point BB is given by

τB=(K)B​8​F​Dπ​d3,\tau_{B}=(K)_{B}\frac{8FD}{\pi d^{3}}, (85)

where (K)B(K)_{B} is yet another stress-correction factor for curvature

(K)B=4​C2−14​C2−4(K)_{B}=\frac{4C_{2}-1}{4C_{2}-4} (86)

and

C2=2​r2d.C_{2}=\frac{2r_{2}}{d}. (87)

When designing extension springs for loads, both the yield strengths of the coils as well as the hooks must be taken into account to ensure that there is negligible chance of failure.

When making springs, spring manufacturers typically prefer the inclusion of some initial tension such that the free length (i.e. unstretched spring length) can be held more accurately. The deflection of the spring then becomes depending on exceeding the initial tension FiF_{i}, such that

y=F−Fik.y=\frac{F-F_{i}}{k}. (88)

The free length of a spring including the end hooks is then expressed as

L0=2​(D−d)+(Nb+1)​d,L_{0}=2(D-d)+(N_{b}+1)d, (89)

where DD is the mean coil diameter, NbN_{b} is the number of body coils, and CC is the spring index. Note that this assumes that the hook has the same diameter as the coils. For the number of active coils for a spring with ordinary end loops (e.g. Fig. G.11) is given by

Na=Nb+GE,N_{a}=N_{b}+\frac{G}{E}, (90)

where GG is again the modulus of rigidity, and EE is the elastic modulus.

Practically, spring manufacturers tend to have a preferred range for what initial tension to lock in for a spring to ensure that the winding process of the wire to create the spring is easily repeatable (i.e. easy to do with the usual equipment available). The preferred range can be expressed in terms of the uncorrected torsional stress

τi=231.0exp⁡(0.105​C)±6.895​(4−C−36.5)​MPa.\tau_{i}=\frac{231.0}{\exp(0.105C)}\pm 6.895\left(4-\frac{C-3}{6.5}\right)\ \mathrm{MPa}. (91)

Equivalently, we can plug in the uncorrected torsional stress τ=8​Fi​D/(π​d3)\tau=8F_{i}D/(\pi d^{3}) to directly calculate the preferred range of initial tension

Fi=π​d38​D​τi.F_{i}=\frac{\pi d^{3}}{8D}\tau_{i}. (92)
Safety Factors

To ensure our system is safe (i.e. the spring system is highly unlikely to fail and drop our detectors inside our dilution refrigerator), we need to keep track of the various safety factors for the various stresses in the system (both the body coils and the hooks). Generally, this is the ratio between the maximum allowable stress of the spring material to the expected stress from the hanging load.

For various materials, the minimum tensile strength can be represented by

Su​t=AdmS_{ut}=\frac{A}{d^{m}} (93)

where AA and mm are fitted constants to empirical data. In Table 1, we show the corresponding values for various wire diameters of phosphor bronze spring wires. For various failure modes, the safety factor will be different, such that we must calculate it for three different cases: failure of the spring body, failure due to bending of the spring hook at point AA in Fig. G.11, and failure due to bending of the spring hook at point BB in Fig. G.11. For a nonferrous alloy (e.g. phosphor bronze), the maximum allowable stresses in percent of minimum tensile strength are 35%35\%, 55%55\%, and 30%30\%, respectively. Thus, the safety factors nn to keep track of when designing extension springs are

n={0.35​Su​tτmaxfailure​at​body0.55​Su​tσAfailure​at​A0.30​Su​tτBfailure​at​B.n=\begin{cases}\frac{0.35S_{ut}}{\tau_{\mathrm{max}}}&\mathrm{failure\ at\ body}\\ \frac{0.55S_{ut}}{\sigma_{A}}&\mathrm{failure\ at\ }A\\ \frac{0.30S_{ut}}{\tau_{B}}&\mathrm{failure\ at\ }B\\ \end{cases}. (94)

2 Geometric Constraints and Expected Load

Starting with the geometric constraints (Fig. G.12), we have that the fridge has 61​cm61\,\mathrm{cm} of vertical space (from mixing chamber to bottom of the 1​K1\,\mathrm{K} can) and a horizontal space of 30​cm30\,\mathrm{cm} in diameter, and the detector housing that we expect to install to the bottom of the lower decoupler stage has a height of 15.5​cm15.5\,\mathrm{cm}. With these dimensions, we are restricted to about 45​cm45\,\mathrm{cm} of vertical space. Because we do not want the housing to touch the bottom of the 4​K4\,\mathrm{K} can, we will design our springs with a vertical constraint of 35​cm35\,\mathrm{cm}. This allows some extra space to work with in case we decide to increase the thickness of the various plates, depending on how much vertical space is taken by the spring hooks, and to ensure that there is some vertical space for the system to fall in case a failure (which will then be caught be a safety structure, proposed in Section 7.E).

The expected mass of the manufactured detector housing is 18​kg18\,\mathrm{kg}. With detectors, electronics, and other necessities, we will estimate that the total detector payload is about 20​kg20\,\mathrm{kg} when considering spring design. Thus, these constraints in geometry and mass will restrict the length of stretched springs and the radius of the stages, and this must be taken into account.

3 Proposed Extension Springs

With all of these spring design equations to keep track of, we will design our springs using the following workflow for calculating the various spring dimensions and the expected natural frequencies of the system:

  1. 1.

    Choose a spring material

  2. 2.

    Determine the expected total hanging load and per spring

  3. 3.

    Choose a maximum spring diameter DD

  4. 4.

    Solve for the wire dd for a given safety factor for failure at the spring body (use 2, as this is generally the least likely failure mode)

  5. 5.

    Determine the low-end value of the preferred FiF_{i} range for spring manufacturers

  6. 6.

    Solve for the number of body coils NbN_{b} needed to achieve the desired stretched length given the geometric constraints, using the sum of the free length and the expected deflection. Round NbN_{b} down (to stay within the geometric constraints) to the nearest half-integer to ensure that the hooks are in-plane with each other

  7. 7.

    Use NbN_{b}, DD, and dd to calculate the spring rate kk

  8. 8.

    Calculate the safety factors for the hook failure modes (at points AA and BB) to ensure they are 1.5 or greater (a reasonable value)

  9. 9.

    Calculate the expected natural frequencies of the system

One Stage

As the one-stage system will be simpler than the two-stage system, we will use it as a relatively in-depth example of the workflow. For our spring material, we will choose phosphor bronze due to its long history of usage in cryogenics for its good thermal conductance. As will be discussed in later sections, this property is important, as the springs themselves should quickly cool down, such that they do not act as a heat source. For the one-stage system, we will assume that the hanging mass is a total of 20​kg20\,\mathrm{kg}, given by our expected load from the IR-tight housing (Section 2). We next set the maximum spring diameter to D=25​mmD=25\,\mathrm{mm} semi-arbitrarily—given that the stages are up to 27​cm27\,\mathrm{cm} in diameter, the chosen DD is about 10% of this, and the springs can be installed close to the perimeter of the stage. Furthermore, we should remember that our intuition on springs was such that the spring should have the smallest possible spring rate k∝d4/D3k\propto d^{4}/D^{3}, this implies that we always want the spring diameter DD to be as large as possible and the wire diameter dd to be as small as possible.

To solve for dd given a safety factor of 2 at the spring body, we use Eqs. (79) and (94), rearranging as

0.35​Su​tn=KB​8​Fl​o​a​d​Dπ​d3\frac{0.35S_{ut}}{n}=K_{B}\frac{8F_{load}D}{\pi d^{3}} (95)

and solving for dd, where Fl​o​a​d=13​m​gF_{load}=\frac{1}{3}mg. In our case of m=20​kgm=20\,\mathrm{kg} for the one-stage system, we find that d=3.2​mmd=3.2\,\mathrm{mm} is the smallest that the wire diameter can be (any lower and the safety factor would drop below 2). With both DD and dd known, we use Eq. 92 to determine the smallest reasonable initial tension FiF_{i} for a spring manufacturer to be able to fabricate. In this case, we find that Fi=40​NF_{i}=40\,\mathrm{N} for each spring. Comparing to the mass per spring of 20/3​kg20/3\,\mathrm{kg} (i.e. Fl​o​a​d=65​NF_{load}=65\,\mathrm{N} per spring), this initial tension is significant and the deflection of the springs under load will be about 2.6 times less than if there were no initial tension in the spring.

The next step is to solve for the number of body coils NbN_{b}, which will finish up the spring design parameters. Given our geometric constraints of the fridge, we know that the one-stage system should not have a stretched spring length longer than lm​a​x=35​cml_{max}=35\,\mathrm{cm}. Using Eqs. (88) and (89), we rearrange the relations to

lm​a​x=L0+y=2​(D−d)+(Nb+1)​d+8​(Fl​o​a​d−Fi)​D3​(Nb+GE)G​d4l_{max}=L_{0}+y=2(D-d)+(N_{b}+1)d+\frac{8(F_{load}-F_{i})D^{3}(N_{b}+\frac{G}{E})}{Gd^{4}} (96)

and solve for NbN_{b}. For our one-stage system, we find that the number of body coils needed to fulfill all of our requirements so far is Nb=77N_{b}=77. Note that this was done assuming that the hook radius about point AA was the same as the spring radius (i.e. r1=D/2r_{1}=D/2), so we will keep this assumption and furthermore set the hook radius about point BB to the same value (r2=D/2r_{2}=D/2).

In the last few steps, we use all of our design parameters to calculate the spring rate kk and the remaining safety factors related to hook failure. We find that k=440.6​N/mk=440.6\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m} and the safety factors of the hook for failure about point AA and point BB are 1.63 and 1.82, respectively. Thus, we would expect failure to occur at the hooks before the spring body. Nonetheless, our spring design for the expected load should be safe, as the safety factors are far above 1 (i.e. we would have to overload our system by more than 10​kg10\,\mathrm{kg} to cause a failure).

With k=440.6​N/mk=440.6\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}, lm​a​x=35​cml_{max}=35\,\mathrm{cm}, a hanging mass of 20​kg20\,\mathrm{kg}, and stage diameter of 27​cm27\,\mathrm{cm}, we finally return to the natural frequencies that we solved for using the Lagrangian method in Section 1. Plugging into Eqs. (30)–(33), we find that the various natural frequencies are fz=1.29​Hzf_{z}=1.29\,\mathrm{Hz}, fx,y=0.84​Hzf_{x,y}=0.84\,\mathrm{Hz}, fz,r​o​t.=1.19​Hzf_{z,rot.}=1.19\,\mathrm{Hz}, and fx,y,r​o​t.=1.83​Hzf_{x,y,rot.}=1.83\,\mathrm{Hz}. Above these frequencies, all vibrationally-induced noise should be attenuated. Given that the pulse-tube itself oscillates at 1.4​Hz1.4\,\mathrm{Hz}, these frequencies are not exactly that frequency, and we should be safe from being on a resonance. For this proposed one-stage system, the design and calculated parameters are all stored in Table 2.

Two Stage

When determining the spring design parameters for the two-stage system, the workflow is equivalent, but must be done twice. That is, we split up the stages into an upper stage with a total hanging mass of m1+m2m_{1}+m_{2} (the sum of the masses of both stages) and a lower stage with a total hanging mass of m2=20​kgm_{2}=20\,\mathrm{kg} (the mass of the IR-tight housing). Again choosing phosphor bronze, we start with the same spring diameter D=25​mmD=25\,\mathrm{mm} for the springs on each stage. Although m1m_{1} can be any value, we have seen from our intuition that it should be at least as much as m2m_{2} if not more. In this design, we will choose m1=20​kgm_{1}=20\,\mathrm{kg} as well and will later check that a larger mass would not give significantly greater performance (i.e. significantly lower the natural frequencies of the system).

In this two-stage system, we also will ensure that the stretched lengths of the upper and lower stage springs are not identical, to ensure that the resonances of each spring are nonoverlapping. To do this, we make another semi-arbitrary choice and choose the upper stage springs to have stretched lengths of 17.9​cm17.9\,\mathrm{cm} and the lower stage springs to have stretched lengths of 16.9​cm16.9\,\mathrm{cm}. We then follow our workflow to determine the rest of the values, just as we did for the one-stage system. Using the proposed constraints in the previous paragraph, the parameters for the two-stage system are reported in Table 3.

We now return to our choice of m1=20​kgm_{1}=20\,\mathrm{kg} on the upper stage, such that the upper springs together would be holding up m1+m2=40​kgm_{1}+m_{2}=40\,\mathrm{kg} in mass. In order to show that this was a reasonable choice, we can show how the various natural frequencies change as a functional of upper stage mass m1m_{1}. To do this, we simply follow the same workflow for some arbitrary m1m_{1} and report the various natural frequencies which would correspond to the optimal design, with the results shown in Fig. G.13. In this figure, it is clear that the difference between m1=20​kgm_{1}=20\,\mathrm{kg} and m1=40​kgm_{1}=40\,\mathrm{kg} is small, such that are original choice is reasonable. We also note that there is a minimum in both of the highest frequencies such that too large of masses actually begin to increase some of the frequencies. This should not be surprising given what we showed the same behavior in Fig. G.9, from which we would expect worse frequencies for larger upper stage masses after some point for the spring modes.

We have spent most of our time with the eigenfrequencies of the system, but it is worth also checking how the eigenvectors change as we increase the mass (while keeping our springs within the safety factors that we have chosen). Taking Eqs. (37) and (38), we can solve for the ratio of the eigenvector components of the system for the eigenmodes ω±\omega_{\pm} corresponding to vertical translations

Δ​z2Δ​z1=3​klower−m1​ω±2+3​(klower+kupper).\frac{\Delta z_{2}}{\Delta z_{1}}=\frac{3k_{\mathrm{lower}}}{-m_{1}\omega_{\pm}^{2}+3(k_{\mathrm{lower}}+k_{\mathrm{upper}})}. (97)

This ratio of the vertical displacement of the two stages becomes as shown in Fig. G.14 as the ratio of the upper and lower stage masses varies. As we increase the ratio of the masses in the upper and lower stages, the displacement of the lower stage increases considerably in relation to the the upper stage. As our detectors will be installed on the lower stage (and be sensitive to frictional rubbing), it is preferable to keep the displacement small, while ensuring that we have excellent attenuation. Thus, this brings us back to the choice of m1=m2=20​kgm_{1}=m_{2}=20\,\mathrm{kg}, where we have this trade-off of low natural frequencies and small relative displacements of the upper and lower stages.

Appendix 7.C Thermal Considerations

We must make sure the heat flow in our vibration decoupler is efficient, such that we do not have any parasitic power sources that will prevent our system from cooling to base temperature (e.g. 8​mK8\,\mathrm{mK}).

1 Thermal Conductance Between Stages

In our system, we will be using flexible OFHC (Oxygen-Free High thermal Conductivity) Cu braids for thermal links [234] and our designed phosphor bronze springs (which themselves will have some thermal conductance). For these metals, the thermal conductivity can be approximated using the empirical Wiedemann–Franz law, which states that the ratio of the electronic contribution to the thermal conductivity κ\kappa to the electrical conductivity σ\sigma of a metal is proportional to temperature

κσ=L​T,\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}=LT, (98)

where LL is the Lorenz number

L≡π23​(kBe)2=2.44×10−8​V2K2.L\equiv\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}\left(\frac{k_{B}}{e}\right)^{2}=2.44\times 10^{-8}\frac{\mathrm{V}^{2}}{\mathrm{K^{2}}}. (99)

For the electrical conductance of a metal, one can generally use a measured value at room temperature and a measured value at a few K. Usually this ratio is defined using the electrical resistivity ρ=1/σ\rho=1/\sigma, with the Residual-resistance ratio (RRR) defined as

RRR=ρ300​Kρ0​K.\mathrm{RRR}=\frac{\rho_{300\,\mathrm{K}}}{\rho_{0\,\mathrm{K}}}. (100)

Practically, the resistivity of a given sample will be measured at a few K, and the RRR will be determined at this nonzero temperature. Notably, in superconducting metals, the RRR would be defined using the resistivity just above the superconducting transition temperature, as ρ=0\rho=0 below this. For us, we will use OFHC Cu and CDA 510 phosphor bronze, which each have measured RRRs of 77 [234] and 1.24 [235], respectively.

For determining the thermal conductance GG of a metal, we use the Wiedemann–Franz law, measured RRR values, and that the conductance is related to the conductivity via G=κ​A/ℓG=\kappa A/\ell, where AA is the area through which heat flows (e.g. the cross sectional of a wire) and ℓ\ell is the thickness of the metal through which heat is flowing (e.g. the length of a wire). Putting this together, we have that thermal conductance of a normal metal at low temperatures is

G=L​A⋅RRRρ300​K​ℓ​T.G=\frac{LA\cdot\mathrm{RRR}}{\rho_{300\,\mathrm{K}}\ell}T. (101)

Note that, in the case of Cu braids, there may be some empty space between the braided wires. Thus, the actual cross sectional area AA is smaller than what can be measured from the diameter of the braid. This is parameterized by the porosity pp, where the true cross section for single braid is given by A=p​π​r2A=p\pi r^{2}, where rr is the radius of the braid. In Ref. [234], the porosity of Cu braid was given to be p=0.645p=0.645, which we will use in our design.

To thermally connect our Cu braids and springs to the various stages of the passive vibration isolation system, the means of this will be achieved through solid-solid interfaces. Interestingly, the thermal conductance through a solid-solid interface is not dependent on the area of contact, but instead on the force being applied to the interface. This is because the microscopic roughness of the surfaces means that that there are only points of contact, thus adding force creates a better thermal link by increasing the number of points of contact. As discussed by Ekin [236], the thermal conductance of a solid-solid interface can be calculated via the empirical expression

G⁡(F,T)=G⁡(F=445​N,T=4.2​K)​F445​N​(T4.2​K)y,G(F,T)=G(F=445\,\mathrm{N},T=4.2\,\mathrm{K})\frac{F}{445\,\mathrm{N}}\left(\frac{T}{4.2\,\mathrm{K}}\right)^{y}, (102)

where FF is the force between the two surfaces, TT is the temperature of the system, and yy is a dimensionless constant with values between 1.3 and 3, depending on the material. For pertinent values for Au/Au, Cu/Cu, and steel/steel interfaces, we have reproduced the table from Appendix A2.3 of Ref. [236] in Table 4, dropping the row on sapphire/sapphire. Further experimentally-measured values have been compiled in Ref. [239] for various other interfaces.

To create contact between the Cu braids and the different stages, one generally uses screws to create a large contact force. For our springs, we will be using stud anchors, where the weight of the stages themselves will be shown to be sufficient for a good thermal connection. Because these contact forces are in series with the metals, as well as parallel conductances through the springs and the braids, the thermal system will become more complex. In studying this system, we refer back to the relations between thermal conductances in series and in parallel

1Gseries\displaystyle\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{series}}} =1G1+1G2+⋯,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{G_{1}}+\frac{1}{G_{2}}+\cdots, (103)
Gpar.\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{par.}} =G1+G2+⋯.\displaystyle=G_{1}+G_{2}+\cdots. (104)

When keeping track of the various thermal conductances, we will ensure we follow these relations such that our power loads are modeled correctly.

To calculate steady-state power loads after all the thermal conductances have been estimated, we use the heat flow equation between two bodies of different temperatures

P=∫TlowThighd​T′⁡G⁡(T′).P=\int_{T_{\mathrm{low}}}^{T_{\mathrm{high}}}\mathop{dT^{\prime}}G(T^{\prime}). (105)

2 Stiffness of Copper Braids

Because these braids will be a part of the passive vibration isolation system, the stiffness of the braids may have a nonnegligible effect on the spring constants of our springs. The braids will connect between each stage, and thus can be thought of as its stiffness is in parallel in the various spring rates of our phosphor bronze springs. Spring rates in parallel are governed by

kpar.=k1+k2+⋯,k_{\mathrm{par.}}=k_{1}+k_{2}+\cdots, (106)

which implies that the stiffness of the copper braid must be much less than the spring rates of the phosphor bronze springs in order to negligibly affect the natural frequencies.

As discussed in Section 5.1.6.1 of Ref. [240], the simplest idealization of thermal link stiffness is to model the braid as a fixed-free cantilever beam (i.e. one end of the beam is fixed and one is free). When the braid is bent at with a force FF at its free end, the deflection of that end is

x=F​ℓ33​E​I,x=\frac{F\ell^{3}}{3EI}, (107)

where EE is the elastic modulus and II is the second moment of area. For a bundle of small wires (e.g. a braid), the second moment of area would be given as

Ibraid=N​π​d464,I_{\mathrm{braid}}=\frac{N\pi d^{4}}{64}, (108)

where NN is the number of wires and dd is the wire diameter. Thus, the stiffness kk in this idealized case can be estimated as
